issues.legal_issue: A suit primarily seeking partition by a non-redeeming co-mortgagor is governed by the limitation applicable to partition, even when redemption relief is added and contribution is raised as a defence.
material_facts: One co-mortgagor paid the entire mortgage debt and took possession of the property.
The plaintiff, claiming a share in the property, brought a suit primarily seeking declaration, possession and, alternatively, partition.
Redemption relief was added after a remand, and the redeeming co-mortgagor relied on contribution as a defence to partition.
The suit was filed after the plaintiff's entitlement to partition had been denied.
issues.conclusion: The suit remained primarily a suit for partition, was governed by the limitation applicable to partition, and was within limitation.
issues.legal_principle: A suit for partition accrues when the claimant has notice that the entitlement to partition is denied. A contribution limitation period applies when the redeeming co-mortgagor sues to enforce contribution; it does not apply when contribution is raised only as an equitable defence to a partition suit. The Court applied Article 120 of the Limitation Act, 1908, and relied on Ganeshi Lal v. Joti Pershad, Valliamma Champaka Pillai v. Sivathanu Pillai, and Variavan Saraswathi v. Eachampi Thevi.

predicates.partition_suit_by_nonredeeming_comortgag: A person who did not redeem a shared mortgage brings a suit primarily seeking partition of property in which that person has a share.
predicates.right_to_partition_was_denied: The person bringing the suit had notice that another person's conduct denied the claimed entitlement to partition.
predicates.contribution_raised_only_as_defence: The person who redeemed the mortgage invokes the other co-mortgagor's duty to contribute only to resist partition, rather than bringing a suit to enforce contribution.

issues.definition: When a non-redeeming co-mortgagor brings a partition suit after learning that partition is denied, and contribution is raised only as a defence, the claim is governed by the limitation applicable to partition rather than contribution.

issues.legal_issue: A co-mortgagor who redeems the entire mortgage does not thereby acquire a right to defeat another co-owner's claim for partition, but may require equitable reimbursement before the property is divided or possession is delivered.
material_facts: The parties had interests in the same property subject to a mortgage.
One co-mortgagor paid the entire mortgage debt and entered into possession of the whole property.
Another co-owner and co-mortgagor sought partition according to that person's share.
issues.conclusion: The non-redeeming co-owner was entitled to a preliminary decree for partition, subject to the redeeming co-mortgagor's equitable right to contribution.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 92 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a redeeming co-mortgagor obtains rights akin to those of the mortgagee for the purpose of protecting the right to reimbursement; the redeemer does not become a mortgagee or acquire a higher ownership right. The right is limited to equitable protection and contribution, consistently with Section 69 of the Contract Act, 1872. The Court relied particularly on Variavan Saraswathi v. Eachampi Thevi and also considered Ganeshi Lal v. Joti Pershad and Valliamma Champaka Pillai v. Sivathanu Pillai.

predicates.co_mortgagor_redeemed_entire_mortgage: One person who shared responsibility for a mortgage paid the entire debt and thereby redeemed the property.
predicates.co_owner_seeks_partition: Another person with a co-owner's share in the property seeks partition of that property.

issues.definition: When one co-mortgagor redeems the entire mortgage and another co-owner seeks partition, the redeemer cannot defeat partition but may require equitable reimbursement.

issues.legal_issue: The form of co-ownership does not change the applicable rule when the parties are co-mortgagors of the property.
material_facts: The parties both held interests in the mortgaged property and were co-mortgagors.
It was disputed whether a family partition had changed their relationship from joint ownership to ownership as tenants in common.
issues.conclusion: Whether the parties were joint tenants or tenants in common did not alter the applicable law because both remained co-mortgagors of the property.
issues.legal_principle: The rights and obligations arising from redemption between co-mortgagors apply regardless of whether the co-owners hold as joint tenants or tenants in common. The Court applied Section 92 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and relied on the principles stated in Variavan Saraswathi v. Eachampi Thevi.

predicates.co_mortgagor_property_dispute: The dispute concerns property subject to a mortgage and the parties to the dispute are co-mortgagors of that property.
predicates.parties_have_different_possible_forms_of: The parties' interests may be held jointly or as separate undivided shares.

issues.definition: When co-mortgagors dispute rights in mortgaged property, whether their co-ownership is joint or in separate undivided shares does not change the rule governing their rights as co-mortgagors.

issues.legal_issue: The bar on disputing an unappealed remand order does not prevent the Supreme Court, exercising special-leave jurisdiction, from examining that order in an appeal from the decision made after remand.
material_facts: A High Court made an order remanding the case, and that order was not separately appealed.
After proceedings on remand, a later decision was appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave.
The correctness of the earlier remand order was challenged in that appeal.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court could examine the correctness of the earlier remand order; Section 105(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, did not bar that examination.
issues.legal_principle: Section 105(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, does not bar the Supreme Court from examining an earlier remand order when hearing an appeal by special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution. The Court relied on Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Deorajin Debi and discussed Kshitish Chandra Bose v. Commissioner of Ranchi in relation to challenges to illegal or jurisdictionally invalid remand orders.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_post_remand_de: A party seeks special leave to appeal to the Supreme Court from a decision made after a case was remanded.
predicates.prior_remand_order_was_not_appealed: The party did not separately appeal the earlier order that remanded the case.
predicates.prior_remand_order_is_challenged: The party asks the Supreme Court to examine the correctness of the earlier remand order in the appeal.

issues.definition: When a party challenges an unappealed remand order in a special-leave appeal from a decision made after remand, the Supreme Court may examine that order.
